title: Türkiye’s new inflation path relies on weak domestic demand absorbing an energy shock
bank: Central Bank of the Republic of Türkiye
summary: The Central Bank of the Republic of Türkiye forecast year-end inflation of 29.5% in November while retaining a 24% interim target for 2026. The 5.5 percentage point gap is the Bank’s own forecast relative to its objective. Its explanation rests on two forces operating in opposite directions. Weak domestic spending was slowing the underlying rate of price increases and gave the Bank room to cut in October. More persistent imported energy costs, higher assumed food inflation and slower improvement in expectations raised its projected price path. Its forecast assumes financial conditions stay tight enough to restrain domestic demand after the cut. It also depends on support from administered prices and fiscal and incomes policies (overview, pp. 1–4).

Second-quarter GDP rose 1.1% from the previous quarter and 2.3% from a year earlier. The expenditure composition explains why positive growth gave little reason for the Bank to revise its demand assessment sharply. Private consumption fell again on the quarter, investment was flat and net exports contributed as exports rose and imports fell. Third-quarter non-gold retail sales growth weakened further, car sales fell and an annual rise in white-goods sales failed to offset earlier weakness. Card spending flattened and October interviews still pointed to soft domestic sales. Industrial production fell in the third quarter, although services and construction offered some offset. Seasonally adjusted employment declined by 62,000 to 32.4 million. The unemployment rate edged up only 0.1 percentage points to 8.1% as participation fell, while broader labour underutilisation rose 1.1 points. The revisions left the projected output gap slightly higher but still disinflationary throughout the forecast horizon (pp. 1–3).

October annual CPI inflation was 29.8%, just above the previous forecast and roughly two percentage points lower than three months earlier. The food contribution dropped 2.1 points and services 0.7, partly offset by a 1.1-point increase in the energy contribution. Freight, crude, refining margins and the phasing out of fuel-price smoothing all mattered. Extending the transition for petrol until year-end cushioned the immediate impact. Inflation excluding administered prices stood at 28.2%, below the headline rate. Relatively stable exchange rates and soft demand had contained pass-through into core goods, while seasonally adjusted services inflation showed less inertia. Persistently high expectations and administered-price adjustments remained vulnerabilities. Low vegetable-price readings in the final two months of 2025 also meant an adverse base effect could lift annual inflation even as the underlying trend improved (pp. 2–3).

The external accounts offered some protection, but the reporting window matters. Through August, lower gold and energy imports, a stronger services balance and high gold exports helped narrow the seasonally adjusted current-account deficit. The unadjusted seasonal surplus and capital inflows supported reserves over that interval. September equity and government-bond flows turned negative. October preliminary trade data indicated a larger deficit than the third-quarter average, partly as energy imports became dearer. Over the full reporting period gross reserves fell, Türkiye’s CDS premium rose broadly alongside peers and lira implied volatility fell across horizons, while domestic government yields were broadly flat. The combination cautions against using any one of these prices as a proxy for all aspects of foreign funding risk (pp. 1–2).

The Bank projected inflation at 21% in 2027, 13.5% in 2028 and 9% in 2029, followed by stabilisation around the 5% medium-term target. The 2027 and 2028 forecasts coincide with the revised interim objectives for those years. The key change in assumptions was the persistence of the energy shock in lira import prices and in expectations. Energy prices had partly retreated in November, but its durability was uncertain. The Medium Term Program envisaged reduced backward indexation and administered prices better aligned with targets. That coordination was part of the forecast assumption. The report gave no corresponding calendar of future rate cuts.

Implementation had already eased at two distinct dates. Resuming one-week repo auctions on 24 August brought overnight rates down nearly 300 basis points during the reporting period. In September the Committee kept its policy rate at 37%. In October it cut by 100 basis points to 36% as underlying inflation slowed. Chart 1.1.2 shows the average funding rate and market rates drawing back toward the repo rate. The earlier change in the effective price of liquidity therefore matters for deposit and loan repricing alongside the formal October decision. Retail loan growth slowed more markedly, while lira and foreign-currency commercial loan growth picked up moderately. Earlier restrictions and weaker retail demand both contributed to the aggregate slowdown.

Pressure at investment funds prompted liquidity operations with a different purpose. The Bank increased repo funding, revised borrowing limits, lowered collateral haircuts and temporarily restored lira swap funding from 24 September to 6 October. It gave firms room to refinance maturing bonds by excluding redemption loans from the growth cap. Many fund withdrawals went into lira bank deposits, helping sustain their share. The Bank subsequently raised credit-growth limits except for foreign-currency loans amid moderate growth and rising asset-quality risks and provided for lira remuneration on reserves against qualifying non-deposit funding longer than a year. A shift from funds into deposits can preserve the currency composition of savings while changing which intermediary must find immediate cash (pp. 4–5).

Box 1.1 traces how the Bank absorbed securities and what became of the risk. The portfolio began the year at TRY 262.3 billion nominal. Gross purchases of TRY 222.4 billion in the first four months comprised TRY 137.4 billion fixed coupon and TRY 85 billion indexed. After a pause, another TRY 150.8 billion was bought between 20 August and 6 November, including TRY 47 billion of TLREF-indexed securities after fund-market pressure. Together these flows total TRY 373.2 billion. The portfolio stock reached TRY 567.9 billion on 9 November, a smaller increase than gross purchases because securities also matured. Box Chart 1 puts stocks and purchases on different axes. The portfolio reached 4.6% of analytical balance-sheet assets and its weighted-average maturity rose from 2.9 to 3.6 years. Its initial 2026 target of TRY 450 billion had explicitly allowed additional purchases.

The Bank judged that targeted buying helped restore bond-market functioning. Box Charts 4 and 5 provide a more qualified reading. Ten-trading-day volatility of the two-year yield receded after pronounced March stress and a smaller September spike. The debt-weighted five-day average clean price of indexed securities moved closer to par at times, yet ended below 100. A reduction in yield volatility and a continuing price discount can coexist. These time series track outcomes during the intervention and provide no untreated comparison. An investor evaluating the purchases should distinguish executable liquidity and price formation from a guarantee of par or a forecast of lower policy rates. The Bank expected to detail its portfolio plans in its December monetary policy document.

questions.question: How much of the underlying slowdown survives a renewed increase in lira energy costs?
questions.detail: Demand weakness and currency stability had limited pass-through, while annual base effects and administered prices could obscure it. Compare seasonally adjusted core goods and services, fuel-price schedules, refining margins and firm price expectations in subsequent official releases. The persistence of broad price pressure matters more to the projected rate path than a single headline print.

questions.question: What would make the revised 2027 objective credible to price setters?
questions.detail: The forecast assumes fiscal, incomes and monetary policies work together. The overview gives no quantified contribution for each. Compare the Medium Term Program’s administered-price timetable, wage and tax adjustments, the Bank’s survey distributions and the chronology of implementation. A persistent gap between those assumptions and private pricing would change the risk around the 21% projection.

questions.question: Did purchases restore tradable liquidity in the stressed securities?
questions.detail: The overview shows volatility and clean prices, while flows, maturities and the policy rate changed concurrently. Compare targeted and similar untargeted bonds using auction allocations, turnover, bid–ask spreads and fund redemptions by date. That evidence would help distinguish a lasting improvement in execution from temporary official demand.

questions.question: Where did the benefit of lower effective funding rates go?
questions.detail: Funding costs fell in August and the policy rate in October, while retail and commercial credit diverged. Compare deposit and new-loan rates by tenor and borrower, bank funding maturities and refinancing shares. This would clarify whether easier liquidity mostly reduced rollover risk or was already generating additional expenditure.

limitation: This covers the complete ten-page English Overview, including Box 1.1. The Governor’s briefing and other separately published Inflation Report material have their own publication identities.
